title: Rethink Technology business briefs for January 19, 2018. The
text:
Rethink Technology business briefs for January 19, 2018.
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act impacts on Apple Workers at a Finisar plant. Apple recently awarded Finisar $390 million from its Advanced Manufacturing Fund. Source: Apple 
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act , as the new US tax law is known, has given Apple ( AAPL ) most of what it has wanted in the way of tax reform. The law provides a much lower corporate income tax rate of 21%. It also provides a one-time only repatriation rate for overseas profits of 15.5% on cash and equivalents.
Apple responded to the new tax law and longstanding political pressure to increase domestic investment with a pledge to make a $350 billion "contribution" to the US economy over the next five years.
The New York Times welcomed the Apple announcement:
Apple, which had long deferred paying taxes on its foreign earnings and had become synonymous with hoarding money overseas, unveiled plans on Wednesday that would bring back the vast majority of the $252 billion in cash that it held abroad and said it would make a sizable investment in the United States.
The impression that Apple plans to use its overseas cash to fund the $350 billion "contribution" seems to be widely shared. However, Apple's plans do not require tapping into the overseas cash, and probably it will be mostly untouched.
How I arrived at that conclusion I will detail in the next section, but first, let me provide some relevant background on the new tax law and its impact to Apple.
While the change that lowers the income tax rate is fairly straightforward, the changes to taxation of foreign profits of US corporations are less so. Before the new law, income earned by US corporations anywhere in the world was considered taxable. Taxes on foreign income could be deferred until the income was brought back, repatriated, to the US. But as far as the IRS was concerned, the money was still owed to the US government.
